messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan's eyes still widened in terror when he recalled the night his father had beaten his mother in their small apartment. He was only eight years old at the time, but the memory of his mother's screams and his father's enraged face remained etched in his mind like a scar. As an accountant, Rohan was meticulous about details, but there were some memories he wished he could erase. The event had left an indelible mark on Rohan's psyche, shaping his worldview in profound ways. He had come to believe that the people responsible for harm often faced no consequences – his father had never apologized or sought help, and his mother had remained trapped in the abusive relationship for years. This sense of injustice had seeped into Rohan's daily life, making him hypervigilant and always on guard. He would find himself scanning his surroundings for potential threats, his body tense and ready to react at a moment's notice. As he delved deeper into his past, Rohan realized that the memories of that night still had the power to transport him back to a state of terror. He would see flashes of his father's face, hear the sound of breaking glass, and feel an overwhelming sense of helplessness wash over him. These episodes left him breathless and disoriented, as if he was reliving the trauma all over again. Rohan struggled to put the experience into words – it was as if the memories were trapped in a nonverbal realm, inaccessible to language. Rohan's inability to articulate his feelings had led to a sense of emotional numbness. He felt like he had lost touch with happiness, and that his life was now defined by misery. He would go through the motions of his daily routine – crunching numbers at work, attending social gatherings – but everything felt hollow and unfulfilling. His negative appraisals of himself and the world around him had created a self-reinforcing cycle. The more he ruminated on his past, the more threatening the present seemed to become. As Rohan navigated his daily life, he found that even mundane tasks could trigger a cascade of memories and emotions. A loud noise at work would send his heart racing, transporting him back to the night of the beating. His body would react as if it was still in danger, tense and ready to flee. These physical reactions reinforced Rohan's sense of hypervigilance, making him even more attuned to potential threats. Rohan's relationship with his ex-wife had suffered greatly due to his inability to shake off these memories. He would become withdrawn and isolated, unable to connect with her on an emotional level. His fear of being helpless in the face of danger had also led him to avoid intimate relationships altogether – he felt like he was perpetually stuck in a state of "what if?" The weight of his past experiences had accumulated over time, making it difficult for Rohan to imagine a future free from anxiety and fear. It wasn't until Rohan's best friend staged an intervention that he realized the extent of his struggles. His friend pointed out that Rohan's avoidance behaviors were affecting not just his personal relationships but also his performance at work. The final straw came when Rohan's boss expressed concerns about his increasingly erratic behavior, suggesting that he take a leave of absence to seek help. For the first time in years, Rohan felt like he was staring into the abyss, forced to confront the memories and emotions he had been trying to keep at bay. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he hoped that therapy could help him break free from the cycle of fear and anxiety that had defined his life for so long.
